mcqs.question: Why does re-reading your own code for correctness catch fewer bugs than tracing an actual test case through it?
options: Re-reading is always slower than tracing, so it's a time trade-off rather than a coverage difference
Compilers already catch every bug a re-read would find, making tracing redundant
Re-reading only works for recursive solutions, not iterative ones
Re-reading tends to confirm your intended mental model rather than the code's literal, actual behavior
mcqs.explanation: You wrote the code to match what you intended, so reading it back mostly re-confirms that intent rather than exposing where the literal code diverges from it — which is exactly where bugs like off-by-ones hide. It's not primarily a speed trade-off, compilers don't catch logic errors like wrong bounds, and the issue applies to iterative code just as much as recursive.

mcqs.question: Why should you pick two or three test cases relevant to the specific problem rather than mechanically running every item on a standard checklist?
options: The checklist is a menu of stress points, and not every problem is vulnerable to every one — relevance to this logic is what matters, not coverage of the list itself
Running more cases than the interviewer expects is seen negatively
A standard checklist item is never actually useful for any given problem
Only the empty-input case is ever worth testing
mcqs.explanation: The checklist names common stress points, but a given problem's logic might only be vulnerable to a subset of them — picking the relevant ones is more valuable than mechanically running all five regardless of fit. Running more cases isn't penalized, and no single case like empty-input covers every bug class.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between "mentally simulating what the code should do" and "tracing the code exactly as written"?
options: There's no real difference — both catch the same bugs
Mental simulation is only useful for recursive code
Tracing exactly as written is only necessary when a compiler isn't available
Tracing exactly as written executes the literal line, so a typo like `<=` instead of `<` gets caught; mental simulation reproduces your intended logic and misses exactly that kind of mistake
mcqs.explanation: Intent-based mental simulation runs the version of the code you meant to write, which is precisely why it fails to catch a typo that changed the actual boundary condition. Both approaches matter regardless of whether code is recursive, and tracing exactly as written is valuable even with a compiler present since compilers don't catch logic errors.

mcqs.question: Which of these is an example of the "mutation during iteration" bug class?
options: Calling `list.pop(i)` inside a `for i in range(len(list))` loop, which shifts remaining elements while the loop index keeps advancing
Summing values in a way that silently overflows a fixed-width integer type
Starting a loop at index 1 instead of index 0
Passing a list by reference when a copy was intended
mcqs.explanation: Popping from a list mid-iteration shifts every later element's index left while the loop counter keeps incrementing normally, causing elements to be skipped — the defining shape of this bug class. Integer overflow, off-by-one loop starts, and reference-vs-copy mistakes are each their own distinct bug class covered separately on this slide.

mcqs.question: In the traced `remove_evens` example, what does the trace reveal that a simple read-through wouldn't?
options: The function is correct but has the wrong time complexity
The bug only appears when the input list is empty
The function has no bugs at all on any input
The loop variable `i` and the list's actual indices desync after a `pop`, which can silently skip elements on inputs like `[2, 4, 3]` even though `[2, 3, 4]` happens to return the right answer
mcqs.explanation: Tracing `[2, 3, 4]` line by line shows the index and list contents drift apart after the first pop, and while that specific input still returns a correct-looking result, a different arrangement like `[2, 4, 3]` would skip an element — a bug only a literal trace surfaces, not a read-through. The bug isn't about empty input or complexity; it's a correctness issue on non-empty input.

mcqs.question: A candidate's code crashes on empty input, so they add `if len(nums) == 0: return []` and move on without further checking. What's the risk with this fix?
options: This kind of fix is only a problem if the interviewer explicitly points it out
It patches the specific symptom without checking whether the same underlying assumption breaks other inputs too, which is exactly the "happy path only" pitfall in a different guise
The fix is wrong because empty input should always be rejected as invalid, never handled
There is no risk — the crash is now handled and testing is complete
mcqs.explanation: Special-casing the exact failing input without asking why it failed often leaves the same root cause intact for other inputs that weren't tested — real coverage means checking whether the underlying assumption (like indexing into an assumed non-empty list) is safe elsewhere too. Handling empty input is often the right behavior, and the risk exists whether or not the interviewer calls it out.
